butir.teks: Chapter Five: On the Proper Conduct of the Learner and the Teacher. As for the learner, his proper conduct and duties

that are outward are many, but their details can be arranged under ten headings. The first duty: to put the purification of the self from base character traits and blameworthy qualities first, since knowledge is the worship of the heart, the secret prayer, and the inward drawing near to Allah Most High. Just as the prayer, which is a duty of the outward limbs, is not valid except by purifying the body from ritual impurities and filth, so too the worship of the inward and the filling of the heart with knowledge are not valid except after it has been purified from vile character traits and the impurities of
qualities.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Religion is built upon cleanliness." (١) It is so inwardly as well as outwardly. Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 9:28⟧ alerting minds that purity and impurity are not confined to outward things perceived by the senses. A polytheist may have clean clothes and a washed body, yet be impure in essence, that is, his inward is smeared with filth.
Impurity means what is to be avoided and kept away from, and the vile qualities of the inward are more important to avoid, for besides being vile in the present, they are ruinous in the end.

For that reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog." (٢) The heart is a house; it is the dwelling place of the angels, where their traces descend and where they settle. Bad qualities such as anger, appetite, rancour, envy, arrogance, self-admiration ('ujb), and their kin are barking dogs. How, then, can the angels enter it when it is crammed with dogs? The light of knowledge is cast by Allah Most High into the heart only through the angels. ⟦QS 42:51⟧ So too, whatever mercy of the sciences is sent to hearts is only taken in charge by the angels entrusted with it, who are the sanctified, the purified, free of blameworthy qualities. They look only upon what is good, and with the treasuries of Allah's mercy that they hold they make flourish only what is good and pure.

I am not saying that what is meant by the word "house" is the heart and by "dog" is anger and the blameworthy qualities; rather I say that it is an alert to it. There is a difference between interpreting outward things as inward ones and being alerted to inward things by the mention of outward ones while affirming the outward ones. By this subtle point set yourself apart from the Batiniyya, for this is the way of drawing a lesson (i'tibar), and it is the path of the scholars and the righteous. The meaning of i'tibar is that what is mentioned is crossed over to something else and not confined to itself, as a sensible person sees a misfortune befall another and it becomes a lesson for him, by crossing over from it to awareness that he too is exposed to misfortunes and that this world is on the verge of overturning. His crossing over from another to himself, and from himself to the root of this world, is a praiseworthy lesson. So you too cross over from the house, which is a structure of creation, to the heart, which is a house built by Allah Most High; and from the dog, which is blamed for its attribute and not its form, namely the predatory nature and impurity in it, to the canine spirit, which is predatoriness.

Know that a heart crammed with anger, with greed for this world, with snarling over it, and with eagerness to tear at people's honour is a dog in meaning and a heart in form. The light of insight looks to meanings, not forms.
In this world forms prevail over meanings, and meanings are hidden within them.
In the Hereafter, forms follow meanings, and meanings prevail.

For that reason each person will be gathered in his inner form. The one who tears at people's honour will be gathered as a rabid dog, the one greedy for their wealth as a marauding wolf, the one arrogant toward them in the form of a leopard, and the seeker of leadership in the form of a lion. (٣) Reports have come to this effect, and drawing a lesson bears witness to it for people of insight and vision. If you say, "How many a student of bad character has acquired the sciences!" then how far he is from the true knowledge that benefits in the Hereafter and brings happiness! For among the beginnings of that knowledge is that it becomes clear to him that acts of disobedience are deadly, destructive poisons. Have you ever seen anyone take a poison while knowing it is a deadly poison? What you hear from the formalists is only talk that they patch together with their tongues at one time and repeat in their hearts at another, and that is not knowledge in any way.
Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Knowledge is not from abundance of narration; knowledge is a light cast into the heart."
Some of them said, "Knowledge is only reverential fear," because of His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 35:28⟧ It is as if he were pointing to the most distinctive fruits of knowledge.

For this reason one of the verifying scholars said that the meaning of their saying, "We sought knowledge for other than Allah, but knowledge refused to be anything but for Allah," is that knowledge refused and withheld itself from us, so its reality was not unveiled to us, and what we obtained was only

its discourse and its wording. If you say, "I see a group of scholars and jurists, verifiers, who excelled in the branches and the principles and were counted among the foremost authorities, yet their character is blameworthy and they have not purified themselves of it," it is said in reply: once you know the ranks of the sciences and know the knowledge of the Hereafter, it will be clear to you that what they were occupied with is of little benefit insofar as it is knowledge; its benefit lies only in its being an act for Allah Most High, when nearness to Allah Most High is intended by it. An allusion to this has already preceded.
More explanation and clarification of this will come to you, if Allah Most High wills.

The second duty: that he reduce his attachments to preoccupation with this world and keep away from family and homeland, for attachments occupy and divert. ⟦QS 33:4⟧ Whenever thought is divided, it falls short of grasping realities. For this reason it has been said, "Knowledge will not give you any of itself until you give it all of yourself; and when you give it all of yourself, you are still at risk regarding its giving you only some of itself." Thought divided among scattered matters is like a stream whose water has been dispersed: the earth drinks up some of it and the air snatches some of it, so nothing remains that gathers and reaches the cultivated field.

The third duty: that he not be arrogant toward knowledge nor assume authority over a teacher, but hand over to him the reins of his affairs entirely, in every detail, and submit to his counsel as an ignorant patient submits to a compassionate, skilled physician.
He should be humble toward his teacher and seek reward and honour through serving him.

Ash-Sha'bi said: Zayd ibn Thabit prayed over a funeral, then his mule was brought near him so that he could ride it. Ibn 'Abbas came and took hold of his stirrup. Zayd said, "Let go of it, cousin of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)." Ibn 'Abbas said, "This is how we were commanded to treat scholars and elders." Zayd ibn Thabit kissed his hand and said, "This is how we were commanded to treat the family of our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him)." (١) And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Fawning is not part of the character of the believer, except in seeking knowledge." (٢) So a seeker of knowledge should not be arrogant toward the teacher. Part of his arrogance toward the teacher is to disdain benefiting from anyone except the esteemed and famous, and that is sheer folly, for knowledge is the cause of salvation and happiness. One who seeks an escape from a ferocious predator that is about to tear him apart does not distinguish whether the one who guides him to escape is famous or obscure. The ferocity of the beasts of the Fire toward those ignorant of Allah Most High is more severe than the ferocity of any predator. Wisdom is the believer's lost property; he seizes it wherever he finds it and holds himself indebted to whoever brought it to him, whoever he may be. Hence it was said:

Knowledge wages war on the youth who exalts himself,
as the flood wages war on the high ground.

So knowledge is attained only through humility and lending the ear. Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 50:37⟧ The meaning of his having a heart is that he is receptive to knowledge by understanding. Then the ability to understand does not help him until he lends his ear while being a witness, that is, present of heart, so as to receive all that is conveyed to him, with good listening, humble entreaty, gratitude, joy, and acceptance of the favour.
So let the learner be to his teacher like soft ground that has received heavy rain, so that it drinks it in through all its parts and submits entirely to receiving it.

Whenever the teacher points him to a way in learning, he should follow it and abandon his own opinion, for the error of his guide is more beneficial to him than his own correctness, since experience reveals subtle matters that sound strange on hearing, yet whose benefit is great. How many a patient of hot temperament is treated by the physician at times with heat, to increase his strength to a point where he can bear the shock of the treatment, and one with no experience of it marvels at it. Allah Most High drew attention to this in the story of al-Khidr and Moses (peace be upon them both), where al-Khidr said, ⟦QS 18:67-68⟧ then stipulated silence and submission, saying, ⟦QS 18:70⟧ Then Moses did not remain patient and did not cease pressing al-Khidr until that became the cause of their separation.
In sum, every learner who keeps for himself an opinion and a choice
apart from the teacher's choice, judge him to be a failure and a loser.

If you say, "Allah Most High has said, ⟦QS 16:43⟧ so asking is commanded," know that it is so, but only regarding what the teacher permits asking about, for asking about what your rank has not reached the understanding of is blameworthy. For that reason al-Khidr forbade Moses (peace be upon him) from asking, that is: leave asking before its time, for the teacher knows better what you are fit for and the time of unveiling.
And until the time of unveiling arrives at each degree of the ascending steps, the time for asking about it does not arrive.

'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It is part of the right of the scholar that you not overburden him with questions, not seek to trip him up in answering, not press him when he is disinclined, not seize his garment when he rises, not disclose a secret of his, not backbite anyone in his presence, and not seek his slip; and if he slips, accept his excuse. You must revere and honour him for the sake of Allah Most High as long as he safeguards the command of Allah Most High. Do not sit in front of him, and if he has a need, be ahead of the people in serving him.

The fourth duty: that one who plunges into knowledge, at the beginning of the matter, guard against listening to people's differences, whether what he has plunged into is among the sciences of this world or of the Hereafter, for that bewilders his mind, perplexes his thinking, weakens his opinion, and makes him despair of grasping and gaining insight. Rather he should first master the one praiseworthy path that is approved by his teacher, and after that listen to the schools of thought and the doubts.

If his teacher is not independent in choosing a single opinion, and his habit is only to relay the schools of thought and what has been said about them, let him beware of him, for his misleading is greater than his guiding. A blind man is not fit to lead and guide the blind, and one in this condition is counted among those in the blindness of bewilderment and the wandering of ignorance. Preventing the beginner from doubts is like preventing one newly come to Islam from mixing with the unbelievers, and encouraging the strong to look into the differences is like urging the strong to mix with the unbelievers. For this reason the coward is prevented from charging into the ranks of the unbelievers, while the brave is encouraged to do so.

From heedlessness of this subtle point comes the belief of some weak people that following the strong in what is reported of them of leniencies is permissible, not knowing that the duties of the strong differ from the duties of the weak.

Concerning this one of them said, "Whoever saw me at the beginning became a friend, and whoever saw me at the end became a heretic (zindiq)." For the end returns deeds to the inward, and the limbs are stilled except for the fixed obligatory duties, so it appears to onlookers to be idleness, sloth, and neglect. Far from it! That is rather the heart keeping watch in the very source of witnessing and presence, and constantly adhering to remembrance (dhikr), which is the best of deeds. The weak person's imitating the strong in what appears outwardly to be a slip is like the excuse of one who throws a little impurity into a jug of water and justifies it by saying that many times this amount of impurity is thrown into the sea, and the sea is greater than the jug, so what is permissible for the sea is all the more permissible for the jug.

The poor fellow does not realise that the sea, by its strength, transforms the impurity into water, so the very impurity is turned by the sea's overpowering into its own attribute, whereas a little impurity overcomes the jug and transforms it into its attribute. For the like of this, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was permitted what was not permitted to others, until nine wives were made lawful for him, (١) since he had such strength that the attribute of justice extends from him to his wives, however many they are. As for anyone else, he is unable to manage even part of justice; rather the harm between them reaches him, until he is drawn into disobedience to Allah Most High in seeking their approval.
One who compares the angels with blacksmiths has not succeeded.

The fifth duty: that the seeker of knowledge not leave any branch of the praiseworthy sciences or any type of it without looking into it with a look by which he learns its aim and purpose. Then, if his life permits, let him seek to delve deeply into it; otherwise let him occupy himself with the most important part of it and master it, and take a taste of the rest, for the sciences assist one another and some are tied to others. And he gains from it at once release from enmity toward that science on account of
his ignorance of it, for people are enemies of what they are ignorant of. Allah Most High says: ⟦QS 46:11⟧ A poet said:

Whoever has a bitter, sick mouth
finds even sweet water bitter.

The sciences, in their degrees, either bring the servant on his way to Allah Most High or help in travelling the way with some kind of help, and they have ranked stations in nearness to and distance from the goal. Those who uphold them are guardians, like the guardians of the frontier posts and border forts, each with a rank, and each has, according to his degree, a reward in the Hereafter if the face of Allah Most High is intended by it.

The sixth duty: that he not plunge into one branch of the sciences all at once, but observe order and begin with the most important. Since life, for the most part, does not suffice for all the sciences, prudence is to take the best of everything, content with a whiff of it, and to spend the surplus of his strength, from what is feasible of his knowledge, on completing the knowledge that is the noblest of the sciences, the knowledge of the Hereafter, I mean the two parts, conduct and unveiling. For the goal of conduct is unveiling.
